flawed_step: Step 1, the standard argument, holds: when a vertex v is coloured it has at most deg(v) ≤ Δ(G) neighbours already coloured, so greedy uses at most Δ(G)+1 colours. Step 2 would have to show that the number of colours is at most chi(G)+1 for every vertex order. Nothing in the definitions supports this. The colour greedy gives a vertex depends only on the order and on earlier choices, not on chi(G). Step 2 is false.
counterexample: Crown graph on 8 vertices: a1..a4 and b1..b4, with ai adjacent to bj exactly when i≠j. It is bipartite, so chi=2. Process the vertices in the order a1,b1,a2,b2,a3,b3,a4,b4. Then a1=1 and b1=1 (b1 is not adjacent to a1). a2=2 (adjacent to b1) and b2=2 (adjacent to a1). a3=3 (adjacent to b1 and b2) and b3=3. a4=4 and b4=4. Greedy uses 4 colours, which is more than chi+1=3.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. The general bound that follows from how greedy works is Δ+1, not chi+1. In the crown graph K_{n,n} minus a perfect matching, taking the vertices in the order a1,b1,a2,b2,... makes greedy use n colours while chi=2. With n=4 that is 4 colours, more than chi+1=3.
